opus-5.5.text:
So I find it helpful to place tasks on a kind of two-dimensional map. One axis is dimensionality: how many degrees of freedom you have to reason about, both in the robot and in the objects you're handling. The other axis is fault tolerance: how much error the task can absorb before it fails.

If you look at that map, the easy tasks sit in the corner that's low-dimensional and highly fault-tolerant. Take picking up a box in a warehouse and dropping it into a bin. The box is rigid, so its state is basically six numbers: where it is and how it's oriented. And if you're off by a centimeter, nothing bad happens. You still get it in the bin. That's why industry has actually deployed systems like that.

Now move along either axis and things get hard quickly. Deformable objects like cables, cloth, or bags of food are effectively infinite-dimensional. A T-shirt lying on a table can be crumpled in endless ways, so even working out what state it's in is a serious perception problem, and modeling how it will move when you pull on it is harder still. That's why folding laundry is still so tough, even though a child can do it.

On the other axis you have tasks with very low fault tolerance. Inserting a peg into a tight hole, assembling electronics, or surgery. The dimensionality there might be modest, but being off by a fraction of a millimeter means failure, or in surgery, real harm. Tiny errors in sensing and control, which are always present because of what I call the uncertainty in physics, the friction, the mass distribution, the exact contact points, all of a sudden matter enormously.

And the really hard corner is where you have both: high dimensionality and low fault tolerance. Suturing tissue is a good example. The tissue is deformable, the thread is deformable, and the cost of mistakes is high.

What I like about this framing is that it helps cut through some of the hype. When people see a video of a robot doing something impressive, I ask: where is this on the map? Often it's a carefully chosen task that's more forgiving than it looks, or the demo was run many times and they're showing the best take. It also helps explain Moravec's paradox, why the things that seem trivial to us, like tying shoelaces or clearing a dinner table, are actually way out in the difficult region, while things that seem intellectually hard, like chess, are low-dimensional in the relevant sense and fully observable.

It also points to strategy. You can make a task easier by pushing it toward the friendly corner: designing fixtures, using compliant grippers or suction that tolerate error, or structuring the environment so the robot doesn't need to understand every degree of freedom. A lot of practical progress comes from that kind of engineering rather than from making the robot generally smarter.

r002.rationale: It explicitly identifies the high-dimensionality, low-fault-tolerance corner as the hardest and gives suturing as an example.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So I find it useful to think of any manipulation task along two axes. The first is dimensionality — how many degrees of freedom are involved, and how many of them actually matter for success. The second is fault tolerance — how much error the task can absorb before it fails.

Take an example like picking up a fork and putting it in a drawer. A human doesn't think twice about it. But if you look at it from the robot's point of view, the fork can be in any position, any orientation, it can be tangled with other objects, it has thin parts that are hard to perceive. So the state space is enormous. And then there's the question of what you actually have to get right. For that task, you don't have to be exactly precise — if the fork ends up a centimeter to the left in the drawer, who cares? So it has fairly high fault tolerance along the final placement, which makes it tractable.

Compare that with something like threading a needle, or inserting a key into a lock. Those tasks have low dimensionality in some sense — there's really only one thing to do — but the tolerance is tiny. A fraction of a millimeter off and the task fails. And you can't easily perceive your way out of it, because the error is below what the camera can see. So you have to rely on contact and compliance, feeling your way in.

Then you get tasks that are the worst of both worlds, like folding a towel or untangling a cable. The object is deformable, so the state space is effectively infinite-dimensional — you can't even write down where the towel "is" in any compact way. And the tolerance for error is also low, because if you grasp the wrong corner, the whole fold is ruined and you have to start over. That's why we spent years on towel folding at Berkeley, and we're still not where we'd like to be.

What I like about the framework is that it explains a lot of what's been surprising in the field. Things that look impressive to a layperson — a robot doing a backflip, or a robot arm moving very fast — are often high-dimensional in the motion but very fault-tolerant, because nothing has to line up precisely with the environment. And things that look trivial — picking a coin off a table — are actually very hard, because they combine fine tolerances with uncertainty in perception and contact physics.

It's also a reminder that one strategy for making robots useful is not just to make them smarter, but to change the task. If you can design the environment or the gripper to increase the tolerance — a funnel, a compliant finger, a slightly bigger target — you've effectively collapsed the difficulty, often more than any learning algorithm would. I've always thought there's a lot of engineering wisdom in that, and I'd push back a bit on the idea that we should always aim for the robot to handle the world exactly as it is.

r002.rationale: It calls deformable tasks like towel folding “the worst of both worlds,” explaining their effectively infinite-dimensional state and low tolerance for error.

astra-6.text:
I think of those as two useful axes. One is dimensionality: how many independent variables do you need to describe the object and what you’re trying to do to it? A rigid object has six degrees of freedom—three for position and three for orientation. But if you’re manipulating a piece of cloth, or a cable, the configuration space is much larger. Moving one part doesn’t tell you where all the other parts are going to go.

The other axis is fault tolerance: how much error can you get away with? If you’re putting laundry into a basket, you can be off by several centimetres and still succeed. If you’re inserting a small pin into a tight hole, even a very small error can prevent you from completing the task. So a task can be relatively low-dimensional and still be very difficult because the tolerances are tight.

And those axes are somewhat independent. Cloth is high-dimensional, but some tasks involving cloth are forgiving. You don’t need a perfect model of every wrinkle to pick up a towel. Surgery, on the other hand, can involve deformable material and very little room for error. That’s a particularly challenging combination.

The useful question is therefore not just, ‘How complicated is this object?’ It’s, ‘Which aspects of its configuration matter for this task, and how accurately do I have to control them?’ Sometimes you can make a robotics problem much easier by changing the task or the environment so that small errors don’t matter.

sol-6.1.text:
One way I think about manipulation is along two axes. The first is dimensionality: how many variables do you need to control? The second is fault tolerance: how much error can you get away with and still succeed?

Picking up a rigid object can be relatively low-dimensional. You need to know its position and orientation, and find a suitable grasp. But imagine picking up a shirt and folding it. Now the object itself can change shape in all sorts of ways. There are many more variables, and moving one part changes what happens elsewhere.

Fault tolerance is a separate issue. Putting something into a large bin gives you quite a bit of room for error. Inserting a tightly fitting peg into a hole may involve a much simpler object, but very little room for error. So low-dimensional doesn’t necessarily mean easy.

And these properties depend on how you set up the task. A fixture that holds a part in place can reduce the number of variables you have to worry about. A funnel or a compliant gripper can increase your tolerance for error. That’s a big part of robotics: designing the interaction so that you don’t have to sense and control everything perfectly.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts folding a shirt with picking up a rigid object, but does not compare household object manipulation with logistics package picking.

r002.rationale: It describes dimensionality and fault tolerance as separate factors and gives examples, but does not state that their combination—high dimensionality and low fault tolerance—makes manipulation particularly difficult.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention clearing a dinner table, glassware, or breakage risk.
